screens.title: Queues and Maps
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll explore two companion parts of the Java Collections Framework: Queues for ordered processing and Maps for fast key-to-value associations. You'll learn what FIFO means, how different Queue implementations change processing order and performance, and when a priority-based queue is appropriate. Then we'll switch to Maps and compare three common implementations—HashMap for fast, unordered lookup; LinkedHashMap when insertion order matters; and TreeMap when sorted keys are required. Each idea includes concrete code examples and small design guidelines you can use when choosing an implementation in real code. For example, a print job queue follows FIFO and benefits from an ArrayDeque for efficient operations, while a scheduler that picks urgent tasks first needs a PriorityQueue. For maps, think of a configuration file: if you need alphabetical output use a TreeMap; if you need the fastest lookups and don't care about order, a HashMap is the usual choice. As you go through the screens, notice common mistakes—like using mutable objects as keys—and small method differences that affect error handling. By the end you'll be able to pick and use the right Queue and Map implementation with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next few screens you will build four concrete skills that let you reason about queues and maps in Java. First, you will explain the FIFO principle and how it shapes queue behavior. Understanding FIFO is essential when the order of processing must match arrival order, such as print or message queues. Second, you will compare LinkedList, PriorityQueue, and ArrayDeque as concrete Queue choices, learning when priority or insertion order matters and why ArrayDeque is often the faster choice for simple queues. Third, you will learn the Map interface and core methods like put, get, containsKey, and entrySet so you can store and retrieve key-value pairs reliably in applications. Fourth, you will compare HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap, focusing on performance and ordering guarantees and how those properties affect design. Each skill includes an illustration and a short mnemonic to help you pick the right structure. We will also cover iterating over a map safely and a common error: using mutable objects as keys. By the end you should be able to pick an implementation and reason about correctness, performance, and ordering in practical scenarios.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: These next objectives focus on hands-on skills and safety checks. You'll practice the Queue and Map methods so you know when an operation may throw an exception versus return a safe sentinel value. For queues this includes add versus offer, remove versus poll, and element versus peek. Knowing these differences prevents runtime surprises when a structure is empty or bounded. You'll also practice iterating over Map entries, keys, and values using entrySet, keySet, and values views. Iteration helps when you need both keys and values or when you must transform values in place. Finally, you'll learn to recognize and avoid a critical map pitfall: mutable keys. If a key’s hash code or equality changes after insertion, the map can no longer find that mapping reliably. We'll show you small test patterns to validate your key types and explain why immutable types like string or integer are safer by default. Each objective card includes a mnemonic or tiny visual aid so the skill becomes easy to recall when you write real code.

screens.title: The Queue interface and FIFO
screens.narratorSegment: A Queue in Java models a collection of elements waiting to be processed. The defining behavior for many queue usages is FIFO: the first element added is the first one removed. That pattern is intuitive—like a bank line where the first customer served is the first who arrived—but it has concrete consequences in code. FIFO ensures predictable order for tasks such as printing, messaging, or event handling. The Queue interface provides specialized methods that make these semantics explicit: add or offer to enqueue, remove or poll to dequeue, and element or peek to inspect the head without removing it. It's important to know the small behavioral differences: add and remove throw exceptions on failure, while offer and poll return safe values such as false or null so your code can handle full or empty queues gracefully. A common misconception is that all queue implementations strictly preserve insertion order; PriorityQueue violates that intuition because it retrieves elements by priority, not by insertion time. In practice, choose a FIFO implementation when processing order must match arrival order. Use the offer/poll pattern in production when you want robust handling of empty queues. To practice, imagine email delivery: messages should be sent in the order they were queued unless a priority rule applies. How would you handle retries or transient failures while keeping FIFO intact?

keyIdea.text: Queue enqueues at tail, dequeues at head. Use offer/poll to avoid exceptions and maintain predictable order.

content.html:
Core Concept
Queue and FIFO explained
Queue holds elements before processing. FIFO means the earliest added element is removed first, ensuring predictable service order for tasks like printing or messaging.
Add vs Offer
add throws on failure; offer returns false on full capacity queues.
Remove vs Poll
remove throws if empty; poll returns null.
Element vs Peek
element throws if empty; peek returns null.
Key Takeaway

Use FIFO queues when arrival order matters and prefer safe methods (offer/poll/peek) to avoid runtime exceptions in production code.

Analogy: Ticket line
Imagine tickets handed out at arrival. The first ticket is served first.
Concrete example
<Queue> behavior: enqueue at tail, dequeue at head.
Offer returns false on failure; poll returns null when empty.
Use offer/poll in production loops to avoid exceptions.
Common mistake
Assuming all queues preserve insertion order. PriorityQueue retrieves by priority, so it does not guarantee FIFO semantics.

screens.title: LinkedList, PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque
screens.narratorSegment: There are several common Queue implementations in Java and each fits a different need. LinkedList implements Deque and can act as a FIFO queue or a double-ended deque, which makes it versatile when you need both queue and list-like operations. PriorityQueue orders elements by natural order or a supplied comparator; it’s great for scheduling or when tasks must be processed by priority rather than arrival time. ArrayDeque is a resizable-array implementation of Deque that performs well for most queue or stack patterns and is often preferred to LinkedList when you need efficient add and remove operations without list indexing. The practical differences matter: ArrayDeque avoids per-node allocation overhead that LinkedList has, so it tends to be faster for plain FIFO tasks. PriorityQueue requires elements to be Comparable or a Comparator supplied; forgetting that requirement results in runtime errors. A frequent misconception is assuming PriorityQueue preserves insertion order; it doesn't — it retrieves by priority. Use LinkedList when you need random-access List features or long-lived nodes, use ArrayDeque for lean FIFO/LIFO needs, and use PriorityQueue when priority dictates processing. Consider memory locality, expected operation mix, and whether you need null elements (PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque do not permit null).

keyIdea.title: Choosing an implementation
keyIdea.text: ArrayDeque for fast FIFO/LIFO; LinkedList for Deque/List versatility; PriorityQueue when priority determines processing order.

content.html:
Comparison
LinkedList vs PriorityQueue vs ArrayDeque
LinkedList (Deque)
Versatile: supports FIFO and double-ended operations. Good when you need queue plus list features. Node overhead can be heavier.
PriorityQueue
Orders by priority. Not FIFO. Requires Comparable or Comparator. Ideal for task scheduling where priority decides order.
ArrayDeque
Resizable-array Deque. Fast for push/pop and offer/poll operations. Preferred for simple queue/stack needs due to performance.
Key Takeaway

Match the implementation to the ordering and performance needs: priority, insertion order, or general-purpose queueing.

Use case cards
Print server
Use ArrayDeque for efficient FIFO; low overhead and predictable ordering.
Emergency triage
Use PriorityQueue so higher-priority cases are processed first regardless of arrival time.
Mixed queue and list operations
Use LinkedList when you need queue semantics plus frequent removals or insertions at both ends and list iteration patterns.
Note: PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque do not permit null elements. LinkedList allows null elements because it implements List.

screens.title: Queue code example explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact Java example that uses three queue implementations so you can see their behaviors in practice. The program enqueues strings into a LinkedList used as a FIFO queue, then uses peek and poll to show the head and remove it. Next it demonstrates a PriorityQueue with integers where the smallest value is retrieved first; this shows that internal ordering is based on priority rather than insertion. Finally, an ArrayDeque holds simple tasks and shows how poll removes the head. When you read code examples like this, watch for the subtle runtime requirements: PriorityQueue requires Comparable on elements or a Comparator provided at construction, otherwise you’ll get a class cast or missing comparator error at runtime. Also notice printing the queue's toString representation may not show the internal heap order for PriorityQueue in the same order poll will return elements; rely on poll to observe retrieval order. Practice by modifying the PriorityQueue to use a custom comparator or by replacing LinkedList with ArrayDeque and observing performance and output differences. How would you change the example to retry failed tasks while preserving FIFO for non-priority queues?

keyIdea.title: See behavior in code
keyIdea.text: Use examples to verify removal order. Remember PriorityQueue orders by priority; LinkedList and ArrayDeque use insertion order for FIFO.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Java example highlights
Below is the essential code snippet used in the lesson. Read it to observe method usage and expected output order.
Queue<String> messageQueue = new LinkedList<>();
messageQueue.offer("Message 1");
messageQueue.offer("Message 2");
System.out.println(messageQueue.peek()); // Message 1
System.out.println(messageQueue.poll()); // Message 1

Queue<Integer> priorityTasks = new PriorityQueue<>();
priorityTasks.offer(5); priorityTasks.offer(1); priorityTasks.offer(3);
System.out.println(priorityTasks.poll()); // 1 (smallest first)

ArrayDeque<String> taskQueue = new ArrayDeque<>();
taskQueue.offer("Task A"); taskQueue.offer("Task B");
System.out.println(taskQueue.poll()); // Task A
Explanation and gotchas
  • peek returns the head without removing it, poll removes and returns the head or null if empty.
  • PriorityQueue.poll returns the smallest element by default. The internal array order is not a reliable print order.
  • If you need stable insertion order with priority, consider pairing timestamps with priority in a wrapper object and a comparator.
Try this

Replace LinkedList with ArrayDeque and measure latency for many small operations to see the typical performance advantage of ArrayDeque.

screens.title: The Map interface: key-value associations
screens.narratorSegment: A Map stores associations between unique keys and their values. Unlike collections that hold single elements, a map holds pairs and lets you look up a value directly by its key. This makes maps ideal for dictionaries, caches, configuration stores, and any scenario where you need fast retrieval by an identifier. The core Map methods are simple but powerful: put to store a mapping, get to retrieve a value by key, containsKey to test presence, remove to delete a mapping, and the view methods keySet, values, and entrySet for iteration. Remember that each key must be unique; calling put with an existing key replaces the previous value and returns the old value. A useful mental model is a phone book: keys are names and values are phone numbers. When you need to update a specific entry, use put; when you need to scan all entries, iterate over entrySet to avoid extra lookups. A common pitfall is assuming iteration order; different Map implementations provide different guarantees. We'll examine those guarantees and performance trade-offs in the following screens so you can match your requirements to the correct implementation.

keyIdea.title: Maps are keyed lookups
keyIdea.text: Use Map when you need direct, name-based retrieval. Remember put replaces existing values and entrySet is efficient for iteration.

content.html:
Definition
Map: keys map to values
Think of Map as a dictionary: keys are unique and map to a single value. Use it when retrieval by an identifier must be fast and direct.
Core methods
put, get, containsKey, remove, keySet, values, entrySet.
Behavior detail
put with an existing key replaces the value and returns the old value if needed.
Key Takeaway

Use Map for direct lookup. Choose iteration views that match your need to avoid unnecessary extra lookups.

Analogy: Dictionary
Key is the word, value is the definition.
Example
Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Alice", 95);
scores.put("Bob", 88);
int alice = scores.get("Alice"); // 95
boolean hasBob = scores.containsKey("Bob");
Common mistake
Using mutable objects as keys can break lookups if equals/hashCode changes after insertion.

screens.title: HashMap: fast lookups and key contracts
screens.narratorSegment: HashMap is the default Map when you need fast average-case lookup and insertion. It stores entries in buckets determined by the key's hash code, so get and put operations are typically constant time on average assuming a well-distributed hash function. That performance relies critically on correctly implemented hashCode and equals methods for custom key types. If equals and hashCode are inconsistent, keys may appear duplicated or become unreachable. A classic error is to use a mutable object as a key and then mutate fields used in hashCode or equals after insertion; this can make get return null even though the mapping exists. HashMap makes no ordering guarantees, so the iteration order may change across runs or after resizing. If you require predictable ordering, consider LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order. For most application caches, session maps, and lookups keyed by immutable identifiers like strings or integers, HashMap is the right balance of simplicity and performance. When designing custom key types, write unit tests for hashCode and equals and prefer immutable fields for identity. HashMap: fast lookups and key contracts means hashmap gives fast average performance but requires stable hashcode and equals for keys; avoid mutable key fields.. In practical terms, o(1) average performance and the importance of hashcode/equals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
HashMap essentials
Fast average-case operations via hashing. No ordering guarantees. Keys must implement stable hashCode and equals semantics.
When to use HashMap
Lookups by id, caches, session stores — when ordering is irrelevant and speed matters.
Key Takeaway

Hash-based maps are fast but depend on correct hashCode/equals. Prefer immutable key fields for safety.

Common pitfall: mutable keys
If you change a key's fields used by hashCode after insertion, the map can no longer find that entry.
Example test
// Ensure key equality and hash stability in tests
MyKey k = new MyKey("id1");
map.put(k, "value");
// mutate k's fields used by hashCode -> bad
assert map.get(k).equals("value");
Performance note
HashMap offers average O(1) get and put but worst-case may degrade when many keys collide; a good hash spreads keys across buckets.

screens.title: LinkedHashMap and TreeMap
screens.narratorSegment: LinkedHashMap and TreeMap extend the Map family with ordering guarantees that HashMap does not provide. LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly-linked list of entries in insertion order, so iterating over entrySet returns entries in the order they were put into the map. This is useful when you need predictable iteration such as printing configurations in the order they were added or implementing an LRU cache by using access-order mode. The performance cost is small compared to HashMap because LinkedHashMap maintains a linked list in addition to the hash table. TreeMap uses a sorted tree structure, typically a Red-Black tree, so keys are always iterated in sorted order determined by natural ordering or a provided Comparator. TreeMap operations cost O(log n) instead of HashMap's average O(1), but TreeMap supports range queries like headMap and tailMap which HashMap cannot. Use TreeMap when you need sorted keys, alphabetical outputs, or range-based lookups. A misconception is to choose TreeMap simply to get consistent ordering; if insertion order is sufficient, LinkedHashMap is often a faster and simpler choice. LinkedHashMap and TreeMap means linkedhashmap preserves insertion order; treemap keeps keys sorted. choose based on whether you need insertion order, sorting, or fastest lookup.. In practical terms, insertion order and sorted-order maps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap
LinkedHashMap
Maintains insertion order. Useful for predictable iteration and access-order LRU caches. Near O(1) operations with small extra memory for linked entries.
TreeMap
Keeps keys sorted. Supports range operations and ordered retrieval. Operations are O(log n). Keys must be Comparable or provided with a Comparator.
Key Takeaway

Configuration with insertion order

Alphabetical user listing

screens.title: Iterating over a Map
screens.narratorSegment: Iterating a Map efficiently depends on what you need from the iteration. If you need both key and value together, iterating over entrySet is the preferred pattern because it avoids an extra lookup that would occur if you iterate keys and call get for each. If you only need keys, keySet gives a view of the keys; values returns the value collection when keys are not necessary. When modifying a map during iteration, use the iterator returned by the view and its remove method, or collect changes to apply after iteration, because modifying the map structure directly can throw ConcurrentModificationException. A simple pattern for printing pairings is: for each Map. Entry in entrySet, read entry. getKey and entry. getValue. For transformations, use entrySet to set new values via entry. setValue. When working with sorted or ordered maps, remember the iteration order reflects those map properties. A common misconception is that iteration order of HashMap is stable; it can change when the map resizes or across JVM versions. For mutating large maps, consider building a new map or using iterators carefully to avoid concurrency and modification pitfalls.

keyIdea.text: Use entrySet when you need both key and value. Avoid modifying the map directly during iteration to prevent concurrent-modification errors.

content.html:
Process Flow
Choose the right view: entrySet, keySet, values
Pattern: iterate entries
for (Map.Entry<K,V> e : map.entrySet()) {
  K key = e.getKey();
  V value = e.getValue();
  // operate, or e.setValue(newValue);
}
Use keySet only when you only need keys. Use values when only values are required. Avoid key lookups inside a keySet loop to prevent O(n^2) patterns.
Modify with iterator.remove() or collect changes and apply after iteration to avoid ConcurrentModificationException.
Example: printing entries
for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> e : userScores.entrySet()) {
  System.out.println("User: " + e.getKey() + ", Score: " + e.getValue());
}
Tip
When setting a new value while iterating, prefer entry.setValue rather than map.put to avoid extra hashing work.
Check Your Understanding

Why is entrySet preferred for key+value loops? Try refactoring a keySet loop that calls get into an entrySet loop and measure the difference conceptually.

screens.title: Maps and memory/performance trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap is often a trade-off among lookup speed, memory overhead, and ordering. HashMap typically provides the fastest average lookups because it uses a hash table, but it doesn't maintain order. LinkedHashMap adds a doubly-linked list of entries which uses slightly more memory but preserves insertion order and can operate in access-order mode for simple LRU caches. TreeMap stores entries in a balanced tree structure that maintains sorted order at the cost of O(log n) operations. Memory overhead can matter in large maps: LinkedHashMap stores two extra references per entry for the linked list, while TreeMap stores pointers for parent/child relationships in the tree. When your application iterates entries frequently in a specific order, the small memory cost of LinkedHashMap may be worth it. When you need range queries, TreeMap provides headMap/tailMap methods that are impossible with hash-based maps. For caches where memory and speed are both critical, consider using HashMap with a separate eviction policy or LinkedHashMap in access order. Always measure with real data shapes because theoretical complexity doesn't capture constant factors and memory layout differences.

Architecture
Memory and performance considerations
Understand per-entry costs: hash table buckets for HashMap, linked entries for LinkedHashMap, and tree nodes for TreeMap. The right structure depends on whether ordering or range queries matter and your memory budget.
HashMap
Low per-entry overhead, fastest average lookup, no ordering.
LinkedHashMap

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Task Scheduler & User Profiles
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to implement a simple task scheduler using PriorityQueue and a user profile system using HashMap and TreeMap. The scheduler should process tasks according to priority where lower numbers indicate higher priority. Implement a Task class that implements Comparable so the PriorityQueue can order tasks by priority. Task Scheduler & User Profiles
Implement a Task class with name and priority and Comparable so a PriorityQueue orders tasks by priority. Use HashMap for user profiles and copy to TreeMap to observe sorted order.
Starter hints
class Task implements Comparable<Task> {
  private String name; private int priority;

Implement Comparable carefully for PriorityQueue and prefer entrySet for map iteration to avoid extra lookups.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll explore two companion parts of the Java Collections Framework: Queues for ordered processing and Maps for fast key-to-value associations. You'll learn what FIFO means, how different Queue implementations change processing order and performance, and when a priority-based queue is appropriate. Then we'll switch to Maps and compare three common implementations—HashMap for fast, unordered lookup; LinkedHashMap when insertion order matters; and TreeMap when sorted keys are required. Each idea includes concrete code examples and small design guidelines you can use when choosing an implementation in real code. For example, a print job queue follows FIFO and benefits from an ArrayDeque for efficient operations, while a scheduler that picks urgent tasks first needs a PriorityQueue. For maps, think of a configuration file: if you need alphabetical output use a TreeMap; if you need the fastest lookups and don't care about order, a HashMap is the usual choice. As you go through the screens, notice common mistakes—like using mutable objects as keys—and small method differences that affect error handling. By the end you'll be able to pick and use the right Queue and Map implementation with confidence.

Over the next few screens you will build four concrete skills that let you reason about queues and maps in Java. First, you will explain the FIFO principle and how it shapes queue behavior. Understanding FIFO is essential when the order of processing must match arrival order, such as print or message queues. Second, you will compare LinkedList, PriorityQueue, and ArrayDeque as concrete Queue choices, learning when priority or insertion order matters and why ArrayDeque is often the faster choice for simple queues. Third, you will learn the Map interface and core methods like put, get, containsKey, and entrySet so you can store and retrieve key-value pairs reliably in applications. Fourth, you will compare HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap, focusing on performance and ordering guarantees and how those properties affect design. Each skill includes an illustration and a short mnemonic to help you pick the right structure. We will also cover iterating over a map safely and a common error: using mutable objects as keys. By the end you should be able to pick an implementation and reason about correctness, performance, and ordering in practical scenarios.

These next objectives focus on hands-on skills and safety checks. You'll practice the Queue and Map methods so you know when an operation may throw an exception versus return a safe sentinel value. For queues this includes add versus offer, remove versus poll, and element versus peek. Knowing these differences prevents runtime surprises when a structure is empty or bounded. You'll also practice iterating over Map entries, keys, and values using entrySet, keySet, and values views. Iteration helps when you need both keys and values or when you must transform values in place. Finally, you'll learn to recognize and avoid a critical map pitfall: mutable keys. If a key’s hash code or equality changes after insertion, the map can no longer find that mapping reliably. We'll show you small test patterns to validate your key types and explain why immutable types like string or integer are safer by default. Each objective card includes a mnemonic or tiny visual aid so the skill becomes easy to recall when you write real code.

A Queue in Java models a collection of elements waiting to be processed. The defining behavior for many queue usages is FIFO: the first element added is the first one removed. That pattern is intuitive—like a bank line where the first customer served is the first who arrived—but it has concrete consequences in code. FIFO ensures predictable order for tasks such as printing, messaging, or event handling. The Queue interface provides specialized methods that make these semantics explicit: add or offer to enqueue, remove or poll to dequeue, and element or peek to inspect the head without removing it. It's important to know the small behavioral differences: add and remove throw exceptions on failure, while offer and poll return safe values such as false or null so your code can handle full or empty queues gracefully. A common misconception is that all queue implementations strictly preserve insertion order; PriorityQueue violates that intuition because it retrieves elements by priority, not by insertion time. In practice, choose a FIFO implementation when processing order must match arrival order. Use the offer/poll pattern in production when you want robust handling of empty queues. To practice, imagine email delivery: messages should be sent in the order they were queued unless a priority rule applies. How would you handle retries or transient failures while keeping FIFO intact?

There are several common Queue implementations in Java and each fits a different need. LinkedList implements Deque and can act as a FIFO queue or a double-ended deque, which makes it versatile when you need both queue and list-like operations. PriorityQueue orders elements by natural order or a supplied comparator; it’s great for scheduling or when tasks must be processed by priority rather than arrival time. ArrayDeque is a resizable-array implementation of Deque that performs well for most queue or stack patterns and is often preferred to LinkedList when you need efficient add and remove operations without list indexing. The practical differences matter: ArrayDeque avoids per-node allocation overhead that LinkedList has, so it tends to be faster for plain FIFO tasks. PriorityQueue requires elements to be Comparable or a Comparator supplied; forgetting that requirement results in runtime errors. A frequent misconception is assuming PriorityQueue preserves insertion order; it doesn't — it retrieves by priority. Use LinkedList when you need random-access List features or long-lived nodes, use ArrayDeque for lean FIFO/LIFO needs, and use PriorityQueue when priority dictates processing. Consider memory locality, expected operation mix, and whether you need null elements (PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque do not permit null).

Let's walk through a compact Java example that uses three queue implementations so you can see their behaviors in practice. The program enqueues strings into a LinkedList used as a FIFO queue, then uses peek and poll to show the head and remove it. Next it demonstrates a PriorityQueue with integers where the smallest value is retrieved first; this shows that internal ordering is based on priority rather than insertion. Finally, an ArrayDeque holds simple tasks and shows how poll removes the head. When you read code examples like this, watch for the subtle runtime requirements: PriorityQueue requires Comparable on elements or a Comparator provided at construction, otherwise you’ll get a class cast or missing comparator error at runtime. Also notice printing the queue's toString representation may not show the internal heap order for PriorityQueue in the same order poll will return elements; rely on poll to observe retrieval order. Practice by modifying the PriorityQueue to use a custom comparator or by replacing LinkedList with ArrayDeque and observing performance and output differences. How would you change the example to retry failed tasks while preserving FIFO for non-priority queues?

A Map stores associations between unique keys and their values. Unlike collections that hold single elements, a map holds pairs and lets you look up a value directly by its key. This makes maps ideal for dictionaries, caches, configuration stores, and any scenario where you need fast retrieval by an identifier. The core Map methods are simple but powerful: put to store a mapping, get to retrieve a value by key, containsKey to test presence, remove to delete a mapping, and the view methods keySet, values, and entrySet for iteration. Remember that each key must be unique; calling put with an existing key replaces the previous value and returns the old value. A useful mental model is a phone book: keys are names and values are phone numbers. When you need to update a specific entry, use put; when you need to scan all entries, iterate over entrySet to avoid extra lookups. A common pitfall is assuming iteration order; different Map implementations provide different guarantees. We'll examine those guarantees and performance trade-offs in the following screens so you can match your requirements to the correct implementation.

HashMap is the default Map when you need fast average-case lookup and insertion. It stores entries in buckets determined by the key's hash code, so get and put operations are typically constant time on average assuming a well-distributed hash function. That performance relies critically on correctly implemented hashCode and equals methods for custom key types. If equals and hashCode are inconsistent, keys may appear duplicated or become unreachable. A classic error is to use a mutable object as a key and then mutate fields used in hashCode or equals after insertion; this can make get return null even though the mapping exists. HashMap makes no ordering guarantees, so the iteration order may change across runs or after resizing. If you require predictable ordering, consider LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order. For most application caches, session maps, and lookups keyed by immutable identifiers like strings or integers, HashMap is the right balance of simplicity and performance. When designing custom key types, write unit tests for hashCode and equals and prefer immutable fields for identity. HashMap: fast lookups and key contracts means hashmap gives fast average performance but requires stable hashcode and equals for keys; avoid mutable key fields.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

LinkedHashMap and TreeMap extend the Map family with ordering guarantees that HashMap does not provide. LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly-linked list of entries in insertion order, so iterating over entrySet returns entries in the order they were put into the map. This is useful when you need predictable iteration such as printing configurations in the order they were added or implementing an LRU cache by using access-order mode. The performance cost is small compared to HashMap because LinkedHashMap maintains a linked list in addition to the hash table. TreeMap uses a sorted tree structure, typically a Red-Black tree, so keys are always iterated in sorted order determined by natural ordering or a provided Comparator. TreeMap operations cost O(log n) instead of HashMap's average O(1), but TreeMap supports range queries like headMap and tailMap which HashMap cannot. Use TreeMap when you need sorted keys, alphabetical outputs, or range-based lookups. A misconception is to choose TreeMap simply to get consistent ordering; if insertion order is sufficient, LinkedHashMap is often a faster and simpler choice. Remember these core concepts: A Queue models elements waiting to be processed and often follows FIFO so the earliest element is served first. ArrayDeque is a high-performance Deque-based choice for FIFO and LIFO needs with low overhead. PriorityQueue retrieves elements by priority, not insertion order, and requires elements to be Comparable or supplied with a Comparator. LinkedList implements Deque and List traits and is versatile for double-ended operations but has node overhead. Keep these short reminders in mind when you design task processing systems or scheduling logic. If you need ordered processing, pick a FIFO structure; if priority matters, use a PriorityQueue with a carefully implemented comparator or Comparable. For maps, remember three practical points. First, HashMap offers the fastest average-case get and put operations but does not guarantee any iteration order; keys must satisfy a stable hashCode and equals contract. Second, LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order and can run in access-order mode to support simple cache policies like LRU. Third, TreeMap stores keys in sorted order using a tree structure and supports range queries at O(log n) cost. When iterating a map, prefer entrySet if you need both key and value to avoid extra lookups; use keySet or values when you need only one side. Avoid using mutable objects as keys or mutating key fields after insertion because that breaks lookup correctness. These reminders will help you choose the right Map for configuration data, cached lookups, and sorted listings, and avoid common runtime traps.
